entry: American writer and television producer. Martin is best known as the author of the epic fantasy series *A Song of Ice and Fire*, which [[HBO]] adapted as the television series *Game of Thrones* and its prequel *House of the Dragon*. He also contributed to the shared-world anthology series *Wild Cards* and to the video game *Elden Ring*. In 2005 Lev Grossman of *Time* called him "the American Tolkien." He is a longtime resident of [[Santa Fe, New Mexico]].

United States Army general in World War II. Patton led the Seventh Army in the Allied invasion of [[Sicily]], where he slapped two shell-shocked soldiers and was temporarily removed from battlefield command. After the Allied invasion of [[Normandy]] in June 1944, he commanded the Third Army, which drove across France and relieved American troops at Bastogne during the [[Battle of the Bulge]]. As military governor of [[Bavaria]] after the war, he was relieved for aggressive statements toward the [[Soviet Union]] and for questioning denazification. He also held antisemitic views and made derogatory statements about Jewish people.

Hungarian and American investor and philanthropist. Soros survived the Nazi occupation of Hungary as a teenager and studied philosophy at the [[London School of Economics]]. He began his career at British and American merchant banks before founding hedge funds, including Double Eagle in 1969, which was renamed Quantum Fund. His short sale of pounds sterling during the 1992 Black Wednesday currency crisis earned him the nickname "The Man Who Broke the Bank of England." He has donated more than $32 billion, mainly through the Open Society Foundations, which support progressive and liberal causes. Several governments, including those of Hungary and Russia, have accused him of financing opposition movements. Far-right theorists have promoted claims that he is a "puppet master" behind global plots; these portrayals have been denounced as antisemitic conspiracy theories.

American television host and former Democratic political adviser. Stephanopoulos was communications director for [[Bill Clinton]]'s 1992 presidential campaign and then White House communications director. He was later senior adviser for policy and strategy, leaving the [[White House]] in December 1996. He then moved into journalism at ABC News, where he co-anchors *Good Morning America* and hosts *This Week*. He graduated from [[Columbia University]] and, as a Rhodes Scholar, earned a master's degree in theology at the [[University of Oxford]].

English civil and mechanical engineer, known as the "Father of Railways." Stephenson devised a miner's safety lamp by trial and error, working on the same problem as the scientist [[Humphry Davy]]. His chosen rail gauge, sometimes called the "Stephenson gauge," was the basis for the 4-foot-8+1⁄2-inch (1.435 m) standard gauge used by most of the world's railways. The *Locomotion No. 1*, built by the company of Stephenson and his son Robert, was the first [[Steam locomotive|steam locomotive]] to carry passengers on a public rail line, the Stockton and Darlington Railway, in 1825. He also built the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in 1830, the first public inter-city railway in the world to use locomotives. Rail transport, which he pioneered, was a key component of the [[Industrial Revolution]]. He also advised on roadway construction, bridge design and locomotive manufacture.

American actor, author and activist. Takei is known for playing Hikaru Sulu, helmsman of the USS *Enterprise*, in the original [[Star Trek]] series, a role he returned to periodically into the 1990s. He was born to Japanese American parents and was held with his family at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II. After coming out as gay in 2005, he became a prominent advocate of LGBTQ rights. He has also campaigned for immigrants' rights, including through the Broadway musical *Allegiance*, which depicts the internment experience.

King of the United Kingdom and last Emperor of India, from 1936 to 1952. His elder brother, Edward VIII, abdicated in 1936 to marry the American socialite Wallis Simpson. George had a stammer, which he learned to manage with help from the speech therapist Lionel Logue. Buckingham Palace was bombed during the [[The Blitz|Blitz]], and he became a symbol of British determination in the war. In 1948 he relinquished the title of Emperor of India and adopted the title Head of the Commonwealth. He was succeeded by his elder daughter, [[Elizabeth II]].

King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor of India, from 1910 to 1936. The second son of [[Edward VII]], he served in the [[Royal Navy]] until his elder brother's unexpected death placed him directly in line for the throne. In 1917 he changed the royal house's name from Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor, amid anti-German sentiment. In the First World War the empires of his first cousins, [[Nicholas II|Tsar Nicholas II]] of Russia and [[Wilhelm II|Kaiser Wilhelm II]] of Germany, fell. He was succeeded by his eldest son, [[Edward VIII]].

American politician and businessman, 43rd president of the United States (2001–2009). A [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]], he was governor of Texas from 1995 to 2000 before winning the 2000 presidential election over Democratic vice president [[Al Gore]], despite losing the popular vote. After the [[September 11 attacks]], his administration launched the war on terror and invaded Afghanistan to overthrow the [[Taliban]]. In 2003 he ordered the [[2003 invasion of Iraq|invasion of Iraq]], citing claims that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction and had ties to al-Qaeda. He signed the No Child Left Behind Act and the Medicare Modernization Act, which created Medicare Part D. His second term was marked by criticism of the federal response to [[Hurricane Katrina]] and by the [[2008 financial crisis]], which led to the Troubled Asset Relief Program. Scholars and historians generally rank him as a below-average president.

American politician and lawyer, governor of [[Alabama]]. Wallace served as governor in 1963–1967, 1971–1979 and 1983–1987. In his 1963 inaugural address he declared "segregation now, segregation tomorrow, and segregation forever." During his first term he stood in the entrance of the University of Alabama to block black students. He sought the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] presidential nomination three times and in 1968 won five Southern states as an American Independent Party candidate. Shot during his 1972 presidential campaign, he was paralyzed below the waist. He later moderated his views on race and renounced his past support for segregation.

American agricultural scientist and inventor, one of the most prominent Black scientists of the early 20th century. While a professor at Tuskegee Institute, he developed techniques to improve soils depleted by repeated plantings of [[Cotton|cotton]]. He promoted [[Peanut|peanuts]], [[Sweet potato|sweet potatoes]] and other crops as alternatives that could feed poor farmers and restore the soil. Under his leadership the Tuskegee experiment station published over forty practical bulletins for farmers, many written by him, including recipes and advice on preserving food. He was also a leader in [[Environmentalism|environmentalism]] and received numerous honors, including the Spingarn Medal of the NAACP. In 1941 [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine called him a "Black Leonardo." Popular accounts sometimes credit him with inventing peanut butter, which predated his work.

Liberian former footballer and politician, president of Liberia from 2018 to 2024. A striker, he played club football in France, Italy and England, winning Serie A twice with [[AC Milan]]. In 1995 he won the Ballon d'Or and FIFA World Player of the Year, the only African to win both. He won 75 caps for Liberia. After retiring he was elected to the Senate in 2014, then won the 2017 presidential election over Vice President Joseph Boakai, who defeated him in 2023. Supporters point to his pro-poor policies and infrastructure projects; critics cite persistent poverty, fiscal deficits and scandals involving associates.

American inventor and industrialist based in [[Pittsburgh]]. He is best known for the railway air brake, and in 1869 he founded the Westinghouse Air Brake Company. He also pioneered the use of alternating current (AC) for electric power distribution, competing with [[Thomas Edison]]'s promotion of [[Direct current|direct current]] (DC). His Westinghouse Electric Corporation, founded in 1886, won the contract to illuminate the "White City" at the 1893 Columbian Exposition in Chicago, and it installed the world's first large-scale AC power generation plant at Niagara Falls, which opened in August 1895. He also developed devices for the safe production, transmission and use of [[Natural gas|natural gas]], and track-switching and signaling systems. He received 360 patents and established 61 companies, many of which still exist today.

French statesman, journalist and physician; prime minister of France (1906–1909, 1917–1920). A physician turned journalist, he was a key figure of the Independent Radicals, advocating the separation of church and state. After about 1,400,000 French soldiers had been killed, he demanded total victory over the German Empire. At the Paris Peace Conference he pressed for reparations, a transfer of colonies, limits on German rearmament and the restitution of Alsace–Lorraine, and achieved these goals through the [[Treaty of Versailles]]. He kept a harsh position toward Germany in the 1920s, though less so than Raymond Poincaré or [[Ferdinand Foch]], who thought the treaty too lenient. Mutual defense treaties he obtained with Britain and the United States never took effect because the U.S. Senate failed to ratify its treaty.

French naturalist and zoologist, sometimes called the founding father of paleontology. By comparing living animals with fossils, he helped establish comparative anatomy and vertebrate [[Paleontology|paleontology]], reconstructing extinct animals such as the [[Mastodon|mastodon]] and a giant ground sloth he named *Megatherium*. He established extinction as a scientific fact, and in his *Essay on the Theory of the Earth* (1813) proposed that extinct species had been wiped out by periodic catastrophic floods. He opposed the evolutionary ideas of [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] and Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire. His racial studies helped lay the foundation for scientific racism. He examined [[Sarah Baartman]] while she was held captive in Paris, and his dissection of her after death disparagingly compared her physical features to those of monkeys.

French revolutionary and politician, one of the leading figures of the [[French Revolution]]. A lawyer and prominent orator of the Cordeliers Club, he was appointed minister of justice after the overthrow of the monarchy in August 1792. In 1793 he helped establish the Committee of Public Safety, but he later distanced himself from its policies and called for clemency and an end to the Terror. His criticism brought him into growing conflict with the committee, and [[Maximilien Robespierre|Robespierre]] publicly responded to these demands. Danton was arrested in March 1794, tried on charges of conspiracy and venality, and executed by [[Guillotine|guillotine]]. His role in the September Massacres has long been disputed.

French administrator who renovated Paris under Napoleon III. Emperor [[Napoleon III]] appointed him prefect of the Seine in 1853, and Haussmann supervised a radical urban renewal program of new boulevards, parks and public works, aimed at introducing grandeur into the city. He rebuilt Paris above and below ground; by his own estimate in 1870, one in five streets in central Paris was his creation. Sewers were revamped and gas pipes laid for thousands of new streetlights. Four major parks were planned at the cardinal points of the city, including the Bois de Boulogne and Bois de Vincennes. The Paris Opera, designed by Charles Garnier, was the signature landmark of his works. Critics forced his dismissal in 1870, but his vision still defines much of Paris today.

Belgian Catholic priest, theoretical physicist and mathematician. He was the first to argue that the recession of galaxies is evidence of an expanding universe, connecting the Hubble–Lemaître law to the [[Einstein field equations]] of [[General relativity|general relativity]]. He proposed what he called the "hypothesis of the primeval atom," now regarded as the first formulation of the [[Big Bang]] theory. He was professor of physics at Louvain from 1927 until his retirement in 1964. In the 1930s, with Manuel Sandoval Vallarta, he showed that [[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]] are deflected by the Earth's magnetic field and must carry electric charge. He also argued for a positive [[Cosmological constant]]. He received the first Eddington Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1953.

French filmmaker and illusionist. Formerly a stage magician, he led many technical and narrative developments in early cinema, mainly in fantasy and science fiction. He popularized [[Special effect|special effects]] such as substitution splices, multiple exposures, time-lapse photography, dissolves and hand-painted color, and was one of the first filmmakers to use storyboards. He built one of the world's first dedicated film studios, in Montreuil-sous-Bois, and made over 500 short films between 1896 and 1913. His best-known work, *A Trip to the Moon* (1902), was a [[Jules Verne]]-inspired adventure. [[World War I]] disrupted his business, and many of his negatives were sold for celluloid reuse.

French post-Impressionist painter. He devised the painting techniques known as chromoluminarism and pointillism, building images from small dots of pure color that blend optically at a distance. His large canvas *A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte* (1884–1886) initiated Neo-Impressionism and became one of the icons of late 19th-century painting. His earlier *Bathers at Asnières* was rejected by the Paris Salon and shown instead in 1884 at the Groupe des Artistes Indépendants. Disillusioned with that group, he helped found the Société des Artistes Indépendants, and his ideas strongly influenced Paul Signac. Combining a delicate sensibility with a passion for logical abstraction, he altered the direction of [[Modern art|modern art]].

Canadian former mixed martial arts fighter. St-Pierre won the welterweight title in the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship]] (UFC) twice and the interim title once, and defended his title nine consecutive times before retiring as champion in 2013. He returned in 2017 to win the middleweight title by submission, becoming a multi-division champion, then relinquished it citing health reasons and retired. His UFC records include the most title-fight victories (12). He later appeared in films, including *Captain America: The Winter Soldier* (2014).

Capital and largest city of Guyana (pop., 2022: 125,683). Georgetown lies on the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic coast]] at the mouth of the Demerara River and is nicknamed the "Garden City of the Caribbean." It is the country's retail, administrative and financial center. All executive departments of government, Parliament and the Court of Appeals are located there, along with the secretariat of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM). Its British and Dutch colonial architecture includes St. George's Cathedral and the Stabroek Market.

Private [[Jesuits|Jesuit]] research university in [[Washington, D.C.]] Founded by Bishop John Carroll in 1789, it is the oldest Catholic institution of higher education in the United States and the nation's first federally chartered university. Its main campus, in the Georgetown neighborhood, sits on a hill above the Potomac River. It has 11 undergraduate and graduate schools and offers degree programs in 48 disciplines. Notable alumni include two U.S. presidents and two Supreme Court justices, and the university has educated more U.S. diplomats than any other. Its athletic teams, the Hoyas, include a men's basketball team in the Big East Conference.

American modernist painter, called the "Mother of American modernism." Her charcoal drawings of 1915 marked her move toward abstraction, and she became known for paintings of flowers, hills and desert landscapes. Alfred Stieglitz, an art dealer and photographer, exhibited her work in 1916, and the two married in 1924. She lived in [[New York City]] with Stieglitz until 1929, when she began spending part of each year in the Southwest. She settled in New Mexico in 1949 and lived there for the next 40 years. In 2014 her 1932 painting *Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1* sold for $44,405,000, at that time by far the largest price paid for a painting by a female artist. Although her work is often interpreted from a feminist perspective, she did not want to be seen as a "woman artist."

U.S. state in the southeastern United States and one of the original [[Thirteen Colonies]]. It borders Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida and Alabama, with the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the east. Georgia is the 24th-largest state by area and the eighth-most populous. [[Atlanta]] is its capital and largest city. Georgia became the fourth state to ratify the United States Constitution in 1788, and it declared secession in 1861. It was the last state readmitted to the Union, in 1870. Martin Luther King Jr. emerged as a key leader of the [[Civil rights movement]] from Georgia.
